Answer: Thank you very much for this important comment. We have carefully
examined our data and revised our manuscript and Supplementary Data 1 accordingly.
Our original intention was to illustrate how many annotations in RefSeq were
corrected specifically based on our integrated ANI & whole-genome phylogeny
approach. We never intended to overlook previous studies. After careful examination,
we found that our corrections for 60 of the 101 genomes were consistent with the
findings in previously studies, strongly supporting the performance of our standardised
ANI-based species boundary. The remaining 41 corrections are newly proposed in our
study and were not covered in previously studies.
We would like to clarify that the primary aim of our study was not simply to reassess
and correct of the taxonomy of individual genomes. While we fully acknowledge and
support the essential reclassifications presented in the earlier studies, our goal was to
establish a unified, data-driven taxonomic framework integrating genomic,
phylogenetic, and marker-based approaches for reproducible species-level
identification across Fusobacterium. Our study provided a comprehensive, quantitative
assessment of agreement among whole-genome phylogeny, ANI, and marker-based
phylogenies, using the largest high-quality genome set to date for Fusobacterium. As a
result, we defined a genus-specific ANI boundary for species delineation, developed
the practical B&B method for species identification of isolates without requiring
genome sequencing, and refined the annotation of marker-based MetaPhlAn SGBs
through large-scale analysis, which directly aids in improve metagenomic profiling
accuracy. We wish to provide a foundation to improve taxonomic accuracy in future
research, thereby helping to avoid the introduction of further ambiguity and
misclassification.
The taxonomic revisions we present were only one inherent outcome of our efforts.
The high consistency with previous studies in fact validated the performance of our
approach, while our independent, large-scale analysis has confirmed and extended these
corrections.
Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for the oversight of the significant work by
Sivertsen et al, which was published during the final stage of our manuscript
preparation. We have revised the Introduction (lines 54-73), Results (lines 170-178),
Discussion (lines 341-343) and Supplementary Data 1 to properly credit all relevant
studies and to clarify our intention.
2. Comment 2: The authors focus on the elevation of the four previous subspecies of
Fusobacterium nucleatum sensu lato into the four separate species Fusobacterium
nucleatum sensu stricto, Fusobacterium animalis, Fusobacterium vincentii and
Fusobacterium polymorphum. Taxonomically, these elevations are uncontroversial and
in complete adherence to genome-based taxonomic rules. They were proposed in 2017
and formally accepted in 2021.
The current taxonomy of the Fusobacterium nucleatum group has been confirmed in
several recent studies, of which at least three include the new “biological species
concept”/gene flow network analyses in addition to the standard ANI-based approaches
used in the present manuscript, thereby representing more contemporary,
comprehensive and throughout analyses (https://doi.org/10.1128/mbio.00941-25,
https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-024-06825-y, https://doi.org/10.1128/mbio.02989-24).
The paper by Molteni et al. also assesses the taxonomy for the rest of the Fusobacterium
genus. None of these highly relevant papers have been discussed nor cited in the present
manuscript. If ANI-based methods should be further corroborated, methods like the first
derivative of ordered ANI distance method (https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-024-
03443-z) could have been employed, as it has not been specifically used in
fusobacterial datasets yet.
Statements like “However, there are persistent taxonomic ambiguities within this genus,
particularly regarding F. nucleatum (sensu lato)” and “However, a consensus on the
taxonomy and nomenclature of these taxa has yet to be established.” (paragraphs on
lines 48-75) are failing to describe an updated view on the literature.
Answer: We appreciate this comment and the constructive suggestion. We apologise
for any confusion caused. We wish to clarify that, as mentioned above, taxonomic
reassessment including the established reclassification F. nucleatum sensu lato
subspecies was not the primary focus of our study. We consistently support and
acknowledge the reclassification proposed by Kook et al. (Curr Microbiol, 2017), as
we have previously stated (Bi et al. Nat Commun, 2022). Our intention in mentioning
this historical issue was to highlight the complex and challenging nature of
Fusobacterium taxonomy. While experts in the field (particularly those with strong
expertise in microbiological taxonomy and/or clinical microbiology) are undoubtedly
well aware of and quickly adopt the updated taxonomy, a significant practical challenge
remains in its consistent implementation across the broader research and clinical
communities. Given the expanding relevance of Fusobacterium in diverse diseases
beyond infection, mixed usage in literatures and certain mis-leading annotations
continue to create ambiguity. More critically, this inconsistency often fails to adequately
account for the underlying genetic and pathogenic diversity among species. Therefore,
the primary goal of our study was to perform a comprehensive phylogenetic and
taxonomic evaluation to develop standardised, practical solutions to ensure consistent
and accurate species-level identification, both for current applications and future
research. We have extensively revised the Introduction (lines 54-98), Results (lines 170-
178) and Discussion (lines 341-343) to clarify these points and credit all relevant studies.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable and very constructive suggestion
regarding the first derivative analysis of ordered ANI values. We have performed this
analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1) using a similar approach described in Passarelli‑Araujo
et al. (https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-024-03443-z). We noticed that Passarelli‑Araujo
et al. used Mash distance (Ondov et al. Genome Biol, 2016), which correlates strongly
with ANI, to assess genetic discontinuity. Their method is certainly applicable to ANI,
but our implementation is slightly different. Whereas Passarelli‑Araujo et al. analysed
the Mash identities against a representative genome, we included all pairwise ANI
values in our analysis, which we consider a more stringent approach. As detailed in the
revised Methods, we have sorted all pairwise ANI values in descending order and
calculated the first derivative (Δ) of the ANI with respect to the rank position. The ANI
discontinuity (δ) was defined as the maximum Δ among ANI values > 90% (δ =
max{Δ|ANI ∈ [0.90, 1.00]}), which represented a break or sharp change. Notably, The
ANI discontinuity (δ) occurred precisely at the ANI gap we previously described,
supporting that this gap represents significant genetic discontinuity within
Fusobacterium. We have revised the Methods (lines 548-554) and Results (lines 126-
131) accordingly and added a Supplementary Fig. 1.
Moreover, we emphasise that our taxonomic analysis did not rely solely on ANI.
We systematically evaluated the consistency between ANI-based grouping and whole-
genome based phylogenic clustering at species level (Fig. 2). Furthermore, we have
now also quantitatively assessed the topological agreement between the ANI matrix-
based dendrogram and the whole-genome phylogeny by calculating the normalised
quartet score (Fig. 2).
3. Comment 3: In the introduction, the authors are specifically referring to Zepeda-
Rivera et al. and their proposed division of Fusobacterium animalis into clades Fna C1
and C2. This was a suggestion in clear violation of genome-based taxonomic rules.
Soon after their publication, it was shown in two independent publications that Fna C1
was clearly a separate species from F. animalis (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-024-
06825-y, https://doi.org/10.1128/mbio.02989-24). Later it was shown by Sivertsen et
al. that Fna C1 was simply a re-discovery and misclassification of F. watanabei
(https://doi.org/10.1128/mbio.00941-25), and finally this was also acknowledged by
Zepeda-Rivera et al. (https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2025.2514797), although no
formal correction of their paper has been published. Therefore, if the authors want to
mention Fna C1 and C2, it should be immediately followed by a sentence saying that
this was erroneous and that C1 was a rediscovery and misclassification of F. watanabei.
Further, there is a mention in lines 62-63 that in a study by Piccinno et al., Fna C1 was
recently regrouped with F. vincentii in a metagenomic study. We were not aware of this
study, but this is just another example of people failing to keep their databases updated.
If one does not have the correct genome reference in the reference database, many
softwares will assign reads to the closest alternative species, which for F. watanabei
often will be F. vincentii. However, Fna C1 is just a rediscovery and misclassification
of F. watanabei as irrevocably established by Sivertsen et al. and there are no taxonomic
ambiguities.
Answer: We understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the proposal of Fna C1 and
C2 by Zepeda-Rivera et al. As stated above, in our revision, we have acknowledged
that that C1 corresponds to F. watanabei, as established by Sivertsen et al and extended
the context regarding the shifting history of the annotation of Fna C1 (lines 56-73). Our
independent, large-scale analysis provides strong and consistent support for this
conclusion.
Regarding the mention of Piccinno et al work, we have revised the text to accurately
reflect the context (lines 68-70). We noticed that they had attempted to clarify the
designation of Fna C1 through phylogenetic analysis of F. nucleatum sensu lato SGBs.
However, their analysis was mostly confined to F. nucleatum sensu lato rather than
encompassing the entire genus and not genome-wide. We believe this limited scope
prevented them from obtaining a global phylogenetic view essential for correct
assignment of this taxon.
4. Comment 4: Given the small number of available genomes for many Fusobacterium
species and the narrow ANI-gap described, it is not appropriate to call it a “robust” gap.
However, this is not the major problem with so-called “genus-specific” cut-off values
for species demarcations within a certain genus, representing an academic concept of
little biological or taxonomic relevance. What the authors do is simply to find the
species with the largest intra-species ANI variability and the species with smallest inter-
species ANI-differences and then defining the gap between these biologically unrelated
measures as a genus specific gap. The authors fail to adequately define the utility of this
measure. Each species has its own independent intraspecies variability defined by the
actual biological variation within that species, and its own distances to its own closest
neighboring species and those are the only relevant demarcations for that species. A
theoretical composite boundary based on all currently known species and currently
available genomes within the entire genus has no biological meaning and cannot be
used for e.g. description of new species. Also, when more genomes become available
(and they will) and new Fusobacterial species are described (and they will) and some
species are excluded from this genus (and they will) - these boundaries will be obsolete.
They are a snapshot of currently defined species and available genomes.
Answer: Thanks for this very insightful comment. We have revised our wording
accordingly, throughout manuscript. Our original rationale for describing the gap as
"robust" was that species clustering based on this interval is fully consistent with the
whole-genome phylogeny and clearly discriminates all established species. From a
practical perspective, we therefore considered it suitable as a universal boundary
applicable across the genus.
We agree with the reviewer that each species possesses its own independent
intraspecies variability, defined by its actual biological diversity. In fact, since ANI has
been widely adopted for species classification due to its accuracy and practical utility,
we performed systematic, data-driven analyses to link this gap to biological and
taxonomic relevance. As described in our manuscript, the ANI gap was initially
identified through distribution analysis near the commonly recognised species
threshold without prior taxonomic assessment. Then we showed that the gap was highly
consistent with a genetic discontinuity revealed by the first derivative analysis
(Supplementary Fig. 1) suggested the by the reviewer. We subsequently evaluated its
utility as a species boundary by correlating ANI-based groupings with the whole
genome phylogeny (Fig. 2). Furthermore, while the current gap is a shared interval
derived from genus-wide analysis, many species, particular those with relatively large
numbers of genomes available consistently exhibited intraspecies and interspecies
boundaries that closely align with the upper and lower limits of this gap, respectively
(Supplementary Fig. 3).
We also agree with the reviewer’s point regarding the dynamic nature of this
boundary. In fact, we do not expect the ANI gap boundaries to be fixed and they should
be iteratively updated with new genomic data, as now discussed in our revised
manuscript (lines 368-375, 412-414). From a historical perspective, and as illustrated
in our rarefaction curve-like analysis, the current observed discontinuity may
eventually converge as technology advances and more genomes become available.
While the specific thresholds defined in this current study may not capture every
biological variation, our framework, based on exhaustive whole-genome analysis and
validation, offers a reliable, updatable solution for achieving precise species
classification, moving beyond reliance on imperial thresholds that might introduce
arbitrary results. It is also noteworthy that, compared to many proposed single-
breakpoint species boundaries, a gap spanning >0.5% (corresponding to discontinuity
Δ > 0.5%) represented a relatively wide interval. In the work by Passarelli‑Araujo et al.
mentioned in your Major comment 2, many species exhibited lower Δ values (less than
0.5%). Thus, this relatively broad range reflected a significant genetic discontinuity
across species and moreover provides a practical buffer zone for future convergence
and for handling borderline cases in real-world applications (this scenario will certainly
occur as the reviewer correctly noted). Such future convergence does not invalidate our
study but rather indicates an evolving understanding of evolutionary patterns as more
species are characterised.
5. Comment 5: The recently proposed species Fusobacterium paranimalis has not been
included in the analyses. Although it was published outside of the IJSEM, it is a valid
description according to IJSEM with a type-strain submitted to and accepted by two
separate international strain collections (NCTC15132 and DSM119817) and a complete
genome available in GenBank. It has also been included in the ENA/GenBank
taxonomy. It is therefore likely to be formally accepted as a valid publication outside
of the IJSEM.
Answer: Thank you very much for highlighting the recent proposal of Fusobacterium
paranimalis. As mentioned above, we were not aware of this publication during the
final stage of manuscript preparation, and again we sincerely apologise for this
oversight.
We agree that F. paranimalis represents a significant taxonomic update and should
be considered in our analysis. As stated in our manuscript, our primary taxonomic
framework was strictly based on genomes from the RefSeq database to ensure
consistent quality control. As the F. paranimalis genome was not yet part of RefSeq, to
maintain methodological consistency, it was not yet included in the RefSeq-based
analyses presented in the manuscript.
Nevertheless, recognising its importance, we have conducted a complete set of
supplemental analyses on its type strain (Vestland19T) genome. Importantly, it served
as an excellent validation case for our newly developed B&B method, which correctly
identified it as a novel species, with no match with the defined thresholds in the current
reference set. Our whole-genome phylogenetic analysis confirmed that F. paranimalis
occupied a distinct phylogenetic position in the whole genome-based tree (see
Supplementary Fig. 4). Interestingly, a few of its pairwise ANI values with RefSeq
genomes (71.30%--93.51%) fell within the species gap, while all values remained
below the gap's upper limit and midpoint. This did not contradict our findings but rather
provides a practical example of how our framework handled such borderline cases. As
its maximum ANI to any RefSeq genome is still below the gap's midpoint, it should be
classified as a novel species. This case appropriately revised the lower boundary of the
gap. We have explicitly pointed out that the gap derived from the RefSeq dataset could
be revised when considering the inclusion of the F. paranimalis genome. These results
have been added to the manuscript (lines 297-305, 368-375, 447-451, Fig. 6e,
Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Data 7).
This example perfectly aligns with the point the reviewer raised and our discussion
in your Major comment 4. We are truly grateful for this valuable suggestion, which has
undoubtedly strengthened our work.
6. Comment 6: The recently proposed species “Fusobacterium sphaericum” is included
in the analyses. This is a proposed species from another publication by Zepeda-Rivera
et al. It is not a valid description, since a type-strain has not been submitted to relevant
microbial culture collections, and the name has not been adopted by ENA/GenBank.
Also, it is highly questionable that this is even a Fusobacterium, but Zepeda-Rivera et
al. have not included relevant analyses to investigate this (e.g. a POCP-analysis
including neighboring genera). It has round cells (!), grows with large and waxy
colonies, and shows low 16S rRNA (91-92%) and ANI homologies (70-72%) with other
typical fusobacteria including F. nucleatum sensu stricto, the type species of the genus.
It is most closely related to Fusobacterium perfoetens, representing another most likely
misclassified species belonging to a separate genus (see below). Based on these matters,
we conclude that as it stands, the description of F. sphaericum will not be accepted as
a valid publication outside of the IJSEM. It should only be included in the present
manuscript if all these uncertainties are appropriately discussed and/or resolved.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and highly informative comment
regarding Fusobacterium sphaericum. In fact, we were also aware of the observations
documented in the Zepeda-Rivera et al. paper and therefore understand your concerns.
Our decision to include its genome in our analyses was based on the following
considerations. It is a RefSeq genome under the genus Fusobacterium and met our
inclusion criteria. To maintain methodological consistency and ensure an unbiased
screening process, we applied the same filtering rules to all genomes before any
taxonomic re-evaluation. We consider that this is essential for the reproducibility of our
workflow. In addition, the species name was formally proposed in a peer-review paper.
At the time of our analysis, there was no published note or studies clarifying or
questioning its classification at the genus level. Crucially, even if it belongs to other
genus, its inclusion did not represent a flaw of our study. On the contrary, our analyses,
particularly the whole genome phylogenetic analysis along with neighboring non-
Fusobacterium genera in Supplementary Fig. 4, provided evidence relevant to its
placement and offered data for future taxonomic discussion (see our answer to your
Major comment 7 below).
We agree that the points raised by the reviewer are significant. Our results also
support the need for its future taxonomic re-evaluation at the genus level. We have
added a dedicated part regarding these uncertainties in the Discussion. To maintain a
balanced expression, we have now primarily used its objective NCBI identifier
(Fusobacterium sp. SB021), and mentioned the proposed name F. sphaericum only
parenthetically, throughout the manuscript, table, figures and relevant supplementary
materials. Furthermore, we would like to emphasise that our study primarily focused
on establishing a species-level classification framework. In all our analyses, this
outlying species did not distort the well-supported clustering of validated
Fusobacterium species, confirming that our species-level conclusions remain focused
and undisturbed.
7. Comment 7: While the taxonomy within the Fusobacterium nucleatum group is clear,
there are other unresolved taxonomic matters related to species included in the
manuscript that are not addressed. Currently, there is growing evidence that the
clade including “F. sphaericum”, F. perfoetens, and Fusobacterium naviforme (for some
reason not included in this study) are not Fusobacteria, but belong to other genera. This
is also the reason why GTDB as seen in your Table 1, has included a suffix after the
genus name in their genome-based taxonomy (Fusobacterium_B perfoetens). It
indicates that this is probably not a correct genus assignment. Fusobacterium naviforme
is more closely related to Catonella morbi and has been proposed reclassified as
Zandiella naviformis comb. nov. (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10482-023-01921-1), but
this has not yet been formally accepted. Fusobacterium perfoetens is proposed as a non-
fusobacterium in this paper (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anaerobe.2014.06.007). In figure
1 in this paper (https://doi.org/10.1128/spectrum.00297-22), both F. perfoetens and F.
naviforme cluster together with Cetobacterium and Leptotrichia outside of the
Fusobacterium clade and a similar finding is presented here in figure 1
(https://doi.org/10.1007/s10482-023-01921-1). As shown in your own Table 1, there are
also some Fusobacterium_A and Fusobacterium_C species in GTDB. For the
community, it would be more valuable to include the necessary phylogenetic analyses
to appropriately address these unresolved matters, instead of reproducing taxonomy
investigations within the Fusobacterium nucleatum group.
Answer: We appreciate this valuable and constructive suggestion. we have conducted
an extended whole-genome phylogenetic analysis (supplementary Fig. 4), which
included representative genomes from other genera within the Fusobacteriaceae family
as well as F. naviforme (Zandiella naviformis).
We initially excluded F. naviforme from our analysis due to the lack of a RefSeq
genome and its proposed reclassification (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10482-023-01921-1)
as mentioned by the reviewer. We have included the genome of its ATCC 25832 strain
in the extended analysis.
Our result (supplementary Fig. 4) indicated that F. perfoetens and F. sphaericum were
phylogenetically distinct from well-established Fusobacterium species, but did not
show that F. perfoetens and F. naviforme clustered closely together with Cetobacterium
and Leptotrichia, respectively. We noticed that the analysis in the studies mentioned by
the reviewer were based on core gene or 16S rRNA gene phylogenies, while our whole
genome-based analysis offered a comprehensive, potentially more resolved view.
Besides, the Fig. 1 in Bista et al. mentioned by the reviewer contains a topology-only
tree without providing distance information. In Gupta, et al. They just stated “The
species Fusobacterium perfoetens was found to branch earlier than the other three main
subclades of Fusobacterium, which are marked in this tree.” In our analysis, although
F. perfoetens and Cetobacterium have close ancestral nodes, they were also distinctly
related. But the divergence degree of F. perfoetens (as well as F. sphaericum and several
unspecified species) from other Fusobacterium species appeared comparable to that
observed in Cetobacterium. As for F. naviforme, interestingly, we found that its ANI
values to F. gonidiformans were 76%~81%, higher than the reported ~67% to Catonella
morbi. And, it also showed relatively close phylogenetic relationship to F.
gonidiaformans.
Nevertheless, our data clearly aligned with the reviewer’s point regarding the
taxonomic placement of F. perfoetens, F. sphaericum, F. naviforme and several other
unspecified species. Our analysis could contribute genome-scale evidence to this
ongoing discussion. However, the limited number of available high-quality genomes
for these taxa and non-Fusobacterium currently precludes the establishment of a robust,
genome-based genus-level boundary. Therefore, our study remains primarily focused
on establishing a species-level classification framework.
We have added these results and expanded the Discussion accordingly (lines 188-
297, 358-367, 414-416, 441-444; Supplementary Fig. 4; Supplementary Data 3).
In line with this, we agree that a future comprehensive taxonomic evaluation at the
genus level will be essential as more genomes become available.
8. Comment 8: To underpin their claims, studies like this should include a phylogenetic
tree based on whole genome data and not solely a tree based on partial rpoB sequences.
In all figures and tables, it should be clearly indicated which species that are not
formally valid according to DSMZ or other authoritative bodies.
Answer: We would like to clarify that we had indeed constructed a phylogenetic tree
based on whole genome data (Fig. 1C) and have additionally constructed multiples trees
for further analysis (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 4). In fact, the taxonomic framework
and conclusions of our study were primarily founded on the whole-genome phylogeny
and phylogeny of full-length marker genes, not on trees based on partial gene sequences.
In our analysis, the whole-genome phylogenetic tree was constructed from genome-
wide SNPs and served as the key reference for evaluating species-level relationships
and validating the ANI-based groupings. As for the phylogenetic analysis of marker
genes (gyrB, rpoB, znpA and 16S rRNA gene), we use all their full-length sequences,
not partial regions. The phylogeny of the partial region of rpoB (the V1 region) was
analysed only for comparative purposes and lineage classification in relation to our
earlier study that employed FrpoB-seq (Bi et al. Nat Commun, 2022), and those results
are mostly confined to the Supplementary Fig. 8.
Concerning the annotation of species validity, we agree that indicating the formal
recognition status of species (e.g., according to DSMZ) is important. We have found
that adding such annotations to every figure and table significantly impacted layout
clarity and readability. As a constructive alternative, we have added this information in
Table 1.
9. Comment 9: Line 315-316: Which community is this referring to? These matters are
not controversial in the bacterial taxonomy community or in the clinical microbiology
community. Also, this is a political statement that we do not support. Taxonomy is a
rule-based system developed for a purpose. It cannot be based on a perceived consensus
in a vaguely defined “community”. We divide bacteria into species because it is
meaningful to cluster together isolates with the same biological and pathogenic
properties. When taxonomy is changed, it is because we acknowledge that the previous
grouping has been erroneous, and that we are grouping together organisms that should
not be expected to share the same properties. Therefore, it is not rational to dispute
changes like the elevation of former subspecies into separate species. Also, such
opinions stand in direct conflict with what is written in the sentence before: “...and
provides the taxonomic precision essential for advancing mechanistic and clinical
research on Fusobacterium pathogenesis”.
Answer: Thank you for this important comment! It seems we failed to express our
intended meaning clearly in the original manuscript, which led to a misunderstanding.
We sincerely apologise for the confusion caused.
As explained in our answer to your Major comment 2, the updated taxonomy, of
course, could be well-understood and adopted within community specialised in
bacterial taxonomy and/or clinical microbiology. Our use of the term “community”
mainly referred to the much broader and expanding cross-disciplinary research
community now actively engaged in Fusobacterium (particular F. nucleatum) studies
due to its close links to diverse diseases (e.g., CRC). This includes researchers
(scientists and medical professionals) from fields such as oncology, gastroenterology,
immunology, and cell biology, who may not have deep expertise in microbial
taxonomy/clinical microbiology.
To be absolutely clear, we do not suggest that taxonomic revisions should be based
on community consensus. We fully support the established taxonomic revisions. Our
genomic analyses robustly affirm these updates. Our point is that there remains a
practical challenge in its consistent application across the broad community. The mixed
nomenclature in literature (even now) and databases can create confusion, potentially
obscuring the precise correlation between species and their specific biological or
clinical relevance and even misguiding mechanistic studies. More critically, this
inconsistency often fails to adequately account for the underlying genetic and
pathogenic diversity among species.
Thus, the “consensus” is on the consistent adoption and use of updated taxonomy
within this expansive research landscape. The primary goal of our study is to bridge the
gap between taxonomic consensus and its consistent application, by providing a clear
framework and practical tools that enable the accurate and consistent application of the
revised taxonomy across all research contexts involving Fusobacterium. Therefore, our
statement that our work “provides the taxonomic precision essential for advancing
mechanistic and clinical research” is entirely aligned with this goal. We have revised
the relevant sentences (lines 426-428) and the Introduction (lines 87-92) to clarify our
intent as described above.
Other comments:
1. Lines 66-67: What does this sentence mean? You just stated that “Recent studies have
further highlighted their distinctive roles in disease pathogenesis” (Line 54). There is
nothing in the present taxonomy preventing such investigations, although people’s
failure to adhere to or use contemporary taxonomy might definitely obscure such
correlations.
Answer: We thank the reviewer for this comment, which helps us clarify our intended
meaning. The reviewer is absolutely correct that the updated taxonomy itself does not
prevent investigations into genetic and pathogenic diversity. Our point was not a
critique of the taxonomic rules, but an observation about the practical consequences of
using a single, broad name (e.g. the F. nucleatum) in rapidly expanding, cross-
disciplinary fields as mentioned above. Our intended meaning was that persistent mixed
use of outdated, ambiguous, or inconsistent nomenclature in the literature can obscure
the underlying genetic and pathogenic differences among its members. As the reviewer
noted, this is often a result of researchers, especially those from the broader community,
not yet aware of and adopting the updated taxonomy. We wish to highlight a key
challenge that if studies only report associations with "F. nucleatum" without species-
level resolution, it becomes difficult to determine whether a reported disease link,
mechanism, or biomarker is attributable to the overall F. nucleatum sensu lato or its
specific members. This lack of resolution can indeed lead to ambiguous clinical
interpretations and hinder mechanistic research. We have revised the sentence (lines 83-
87).
2. Line 67-68: This is not correct. It is true that the V3-V4 region commonly used for
Illumina sequencing does not discriminate well between some of these species, but
other regions like e.g. V1-V3 or the full gene can be used to discriminate between
most Fusobacterium species, including the currently accepted species in the Fusobacterium
nucleatum group.
Answer: Thanks for pointing that out. We have revised the text to be more precise (line
94). We agree that the full-length 16S rRNA gene or V1-V3 region can discriminate
Fusobacterium species. It should be noted, however, that even the full-length 16S rRNA
gene may not provide sufficient resolution in some cases, as documented in previous
studies (e.g Kim, et al. J Clin Microbiol. 2009) and observed in our analysis.
3. Line 69-70: This is not the case. There are several recent studies addressing this, but
authors are not citing them.
Answer: We have revised the text while revising the Introduction as mentioned above
(lines 73-76, 84-87, 95-98).
4. Lines 127-129: As mentioned above, a range of recent studies have flagged these
wrongly annotated genomes before, but the authors are not citing them.
Answer: Thank you for reiterating this point regarding this text. As detailed in our
answer to your Major Comment 1, we have made revisions accordingly (lines 170-178;
Supplementary Data 1).
5. Lines 132-136: This has already been established by Sivertsen et al.
(https://doi.org/10.1128/mbio.00941-25). This was the main purpose of their study.
They also provided the F. watanabei type strain whole genome used in the present study.
Answer: We acknowledge our oversight again of this very recent work (we were at the
final stage of our manuscript preparation and did not read it in time. Apologise!). As
detailed in our response to your Major comment 1, we have revised the manuscript
accordingly (lines 171-176, 56-73).
6. Lines 139-140: This has also been pointed out by others (10.1007/s10482-023-
01921-1) and is acknowledged by DSMZ.
Answer: Thank you very much for the comment! We have also corrected this while
revising the manuscript in response to your Major Comment 1 (lines 176-178).
7. Lines 142-149: It is fine to conclude that some genomes are probably representatives
of novel species. However, proposing new names based on this is not very useful, since
a valid description of novel species requires a type-strain submitted to at least two

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
The authors analyse 542 genomes of the genus Fusobacterium to better approach the
taxonomy of the genus. They conducted ANI analyses, a whole genome phylogeny, plus
individual gene phylogenies to get a sound idea of the phylogenetic relationships within
the genus. This study has the potential to add some insights into the taxonomy of this
genus. However, there are some major and minor issues the authors want to address in
a revised version.
Major comments
1. To appreciate the quality of the genome assemblies, the authors want to run CheckM
on all the genomes and report completeness and contamination; this info should be
added to Supplementary Table 1. Ideally, for downstream analyses, they just want to
consider genomes with > 95% completeness and < 5% contamination. Also, the authors
need to provide the BioProject of the newly sequenced genomes.
Answer: Thank you for your thoughtful suggestion! We have assessed the quality of
all genomes in our study using CheckM2 (Chklovski, et al. Nature Method, 2023), the
latest version of CheckM and applied the suggested inclusion criteria (> 95%
completeness and < 5% contamination) (lines 436-438). The genome completeness and
contamination data have now been added to Supplementary Data 1 (for the RefSeq
genomes), Supplementary Data 7 (for newly sequenced and the GenBank genomes)
and Supplementary Data 3 (for the representative genomes from other genera within
Fusobacteriaceae). Two RefSeq genomes failed to meet the quality thresholds and were
therefore excluded from subsequent analyses. We have re-executed the entire analysis
workflow with this updated RefSeq dataset and revised all relevant Results, Methods,
figures, and Supplementary Data accordingly. Importantly, all major conclusions of our
study remain fully supported.
Please note that the BioProject accession number (PRJNA704481) of the newly
sequenced genomes was already provided in the Data and resource availability section
of the original manuscript and the related GenBank accession numbers of individual
genomes are also listed in Supplementary Data 7.
2. Considering the concordance between the whole-genome phylogeny and the ANI-
based grouping, a formal topology test (KH-test, SH-test, AU-test, RELL, etc) is
desirable. So, to know if those strategies produce statistically significant different
groupings. Just from visually comparing the topologies, it is not possible to know
whether or not they are statistically different.
Answer: Thank you for very much for the constructive and insightful suggestion! We
fully agree that a formal quantitative assessment of the concordance between the whole-
genome phylogeny and ANI-based grouping is crucial and would significantly
strengthen our study.
We have given careful consideration to the topology tests including KH-test, SH-test,
AU-test or RELL. We recognise that these methods are powerful tools for comparing
phylogenetic trees inferred from the same dataset under different models or parameters
to choose the best-fitting tree for this dataset. In our case, however, we were comparing
groupings derived from fundamentally different data types, namely, a whole genome-
based alignment (used for phylogeny) and a genomic ANI matrix (used for clustering).
These data captured different evolutionary signals (substitution history vs. genome-
wide identity), and thus their topologies and branch lengths are not expected to be
statistically equivalent in a branch-by-branch manner. For this reason, we considered
that direct application of these topology tests would not be methodologically
appropriate here.
Alternatively, to evaluate the topological concordance between the two approaches,
we employed ASTRAL (v5.7.8) to calculate a normalised quartet score (NQS), which
quantified the proportion of shared evolutionary relationships (quartets) between two
trees, making it ideal for comparing trees built from different data sources. The analysis
yielded an NQS of 0.904 between the whole-genome tree and the ANI-based
dendrogram, indicating very strong concordance. We have included the result in Fig. 2
and expanded the Method section accordingly (lines 559-562).
Similarly, we have also calculated the NQS values between the whole-genome tree
and the phylogenic trees based on the 16S rRNA gene, rpoB, gyrB, and znpA, as detailed
in our response to your Major comment 4. Notably, ASTRAL is particularly suitable
here, given its compatibility with multi-copy genes like the 16S rRNA gene.
3. Important details are missing about the phylogenetic analyses. First, many details
about the whole genome phylogeny are needed. For instance, kSNP4 estimates
parsimony, maximum likelihood, and neighbour-joining trees; which method did the
authors select? Please state all the different parameters employed in the analysis.
Importantly, given the distorting effects of recombination, you want to run a phylogeny
just on regions of the genome not affected by recombination. Did you use all the
SNPs or just core SNPs? Second, re the individual gene markers, please state the DNA
substitution model specified when running the gene phylogenies, maybe GTR+I+R?
Answer: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising these crucial points regarding
phylogenetic methodology.
The whole-genome tree was inferred using the parsimony method in kSNP4, which
is recommended by the kSNP4 paper (Hall et al. Mol Biol Evol, 2023), as a simulation
study (Hall et al. Cladistics, 2015) have shown that kSNP parsimony trees are the most
accurate. All other parameters were at default setting.
Indeed, recombination could influence topological accuracy. We understand that
excluding recombination regions is ideal for inferring a robust tree. However, in our
case, over half of the studied genomes were draft assemblies, which were fragmented
and contained missing data, making large-scale, genome-wide recombination detection
and filtering technically unreliable. To mitigate this concern, we have attempted to
construct a tree using core SNPs via the ‘-core’ parameter in kSNP4, as suggested by
the reviewer. However, this approach failed, very likely due to the high nucleotide
diversity across species and the prevalence of draft genomes, which prevented the
identification of a universal set of core SNPs sufficient for tree reconstruction. As an
alternative, we have constructed multiple trees (Supplementary Fig. 2) based on SNP
loci occurring in at least 25%, 50%, and 75% of genomes (using the ‘-min_frac’ option).
Remarkably, all resulting trees showed 0.96 – 0.99 (>0.998 if considering the species
level) NQS to the primary tree (Supplementary Fig. 2). This high concordance indicated
that the core phylogenetic relationships were robust against potential noise introduced
by recombination. We fully acknowledge not filtering for recombination as a limitation
of the kSNP4-based phylogeny in this study and have explicitly point it out in the
Discussion. Importantly, the species-level clustering resolved by the kSNP4 tree was
also consistently supported by the ANI matrix and phylogenies derived from the high-
resolution marker genes rpoB, gyrB, and znpA. Therefore, we consider that the major
taxonomic conclusions regarding species delineation remain robust despite this
limitation.
As for individual gene markers, we have re-inferred all gene phylogenies with IQ-
TREE based on the updated genome dataset. The ModelFinder Plus (MFP) option was
employed to automatically select the best-fit nucleotide substitution model for each
gene by minimising the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). The specific model
selected for each marker is now clearly specified in the corresponding figure legends.
We have now provided a more comprehensive description in the Methods section
and revised the Results, Discussion and figures accordingly (lines 483-488, 492-496,
146-150, 408-412; Figs. 4 & 5 and Supplementary Fig. 2).
4. Finally, considering their top two markers (gyrB and rpoB), the authors want to make
sure these genes are good phylogenetic markers. I would suggest the authors run
topology tests (see Major comment 2) of these individual gene trees (and also a
concatenated alignment of the two genes) versus the whole genome phylogeny and
ensure that there are no significant differences. Also, they want to ensure that those two
genes do not have signals of recombination. Lastly, please report the nucleotide
diversity of these two genes and how it compares to the nucleotide diversity of the other
markers presented in Supplementary Data 3.
Answer: This is also a very constructive and insightful suggestion, thanks!
As mentioned above, we have calculated the NQS between each individual gene tree
(and a concatenated rpoB+gyrB tree, see Supplementary Fig. 5) and the whole genome
phylogeny for topological concordance evaluation. The result indicated that gyrB (NQS
= 0.905) and rpoB (NQS = 0.864) trees exhibited high topological agreement. Moreover,
to statistically compare the performance across markers, we leveraged the distributions
of NQS values generated from bootstrap replicates of each gene tree (see Statistics part
in the Methods). A Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn’s post-hoc tests revealed that
both gyrB and rpoB trees exhibited higher NQS than the 16S rRNA gene tree (both p <
0.05; see Supplementary Fig. 7), further supporting their superior resolution.
We have examined the signals of recombination in all analysed genes with the PHI
test in PhiPack (version 1.1). No significant recombination signal was detected in these
genes except rpoB (Supplementary Fig. 1). A recent study has also reported
recombination in the rpoB gene of Fusobacterium (Molteni et al. Commun Biol, 2024).
We therefore acknowledged in the Discussion that rpoB tree topology should be
interpreted with caution regarding evolutionary trajectory assessment. Nevertheless, its
high NQS confirmed that its major phylogenetic structure remains highly informative
for species-level clustering. In addition, we did not detect significant recombination
signal in the V1 region of rpoB employed by the B&B method.
We have also calculated the nucleotide diversity (π) of all analysed genes (Figs. 4&5
and Supplementary Fig. 6). To compare nucleotide diversity (π) across markers, we
employed a bootstrap-based difference test. For each marker, bootstrap resampling
(1,000 iterations) was performed (see Statistics part in the Methods). Crucially, whereas
the NQS comparison utilised bootstrapping to approximate the sampling distribution of
the statistic itself, the π comparison employed bootstrapping to evaluate the uncertainty
of a parameter estimate. Therefore, for each maker pair, we calculated the distribution
of differences by subtracting the bootstrap π values of one maker from those of the other.
Statistical significance was determined by examining whether the 95% confidence
interval of this difference distribution contained zero. The corresponding two-tailed p
value was calculated as twice the proportion of bootstrap differences on the smaller side
of zero, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. The
comparison results are provided in Supplementary Fig. 6.
Note that due to the draft nature of certain genomes, not all marker gene sequences
were available for every genome in the RefSeq dataset. Specifically, while gyrB
sequences were available for all genomes, rpoB sequences were available for 539
genomes, znpA for 436 genomes (also due to its natural absence in certain species), and
at least one 16S rRNA gene copy for 414 genomes. Therefore, to ensure fair
comparisons, all NQS and π comparisons were performed only on the subset of
genomes that contained complete sequences for the markers being analysed.
We have added these results and methodological details in the manuscript (lines 496-
498, 517-522, 559-577, 213-215, 220-243, 387-388; and the figures and table
mentioned above).

Answer: Corrected (line 134). Sorry for the error.

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Bi et al provide quite a comprehensive genus-wide analysis that
integrates ANI-based and phylogenetic approaches to clarify some longstanding issues
that have arisen within Fusobacterium taxonomy and nomenclature. They further
introduce a practical dual-marker (gyrB and rpoB) identification method and
demonstrate how it can be integrated with GTDB and MetaPhlAn frameworks. The
analyses are extensive, technically sound, and clearly the product of careful
comparative work across what has been a challenging genus. The effort to unify
genomic, phylogenetic, and marker-based approaches into a coherent framework will
represent a substantial step forward for reproducible species-level identification across
Fusobacterium. This reviewer particularly appreciates the authors’ effort to present a
balanced, data-driven treatment of what is often a contentious subject. This reviewer
also agrees that the novel markers outlined here could contribute to overcoming
challenges faced with traditional 16S rRNA sequencing efforts to elaborate on
Fusobacterium species relevant to human cancers.
Nevertheless, I do have concerns about some of the proposed updates, and along with
a single major point, provide some constructive feedback that may improve readability
and decrease resistance within the field for adoption of the authors proposed taxonomy
and nomenclature adjustments.
Major comment: Against a double meaning for F.n sensu lato.
It appears that the authors are proposing to change the nature of what Fusobacterium
nucleatum sensu lato (Fn s.l.) means (at least as understood by this reviewer and by
many colleagues working in this area). Several statements in the manuscript are
ambiguous in this regard and warrant clarification, as they risk introducing additional
significant confusion into an already complex and historically inconsistent
nomenclatural landscape. Specifically, the manuscript seems to redefine F. nucleatum
sensu lato in a way that excludes F. animalis and F. watanabei, whereas in the broader
literature, the term has consistently referred to the entire F. nucleatum complex,
(including these lineages).
These sentences include:
- Lines 129–138, “the two F. nucleatum subsp. animalis clades (Fna C1 and Fna C2)
constitute distinct species… which did not justify the species status of F. nucleatum
(sensu lato)”,
- Lines 252–255, which describe the current subspecies/clade designations under “F.
nucleatum (sensu lato)” as “taxonomically invalid”,
- Table 2, which presents F. animalis and F. watanabei as reclassified species without
reference to their origin within the F. nucleatum sensu lato complex.
This is in contrast to the current established usage of F. nucleatum sensu lato in the field
(eg. Kook et al., 2017; Ma et al 2023, Krieger et al., 2024; Zepeda-Rivera et al., 2025)
encompasses the four canonical F. nucleatum subspecies (nucleatum, polymorphum,
vincentii, animalis) and their derivative lineages, forming a coherent monophyletic
group sharing ~90–94 % ANI.
It is also important to note that the sensu lato designation functions not as a formal
species rank but as a conceptual and practical umbrella, and is useful to preserve
interpretive continuity across genomic, ecological, and clinical research where
subspecies resolution was unavailable.
This current framework is also relatively well established, as it provides an inclusive
and pragmatic way to refer to the entire F. nucleatum complex by linking historical
culture-based and 16S-based studies with more recent updated genome-resolved
analyses. It is also a default interpretive construct; even as individual lineages are
refined to species rank.
Could the authors please carefully consider and explicitly outline what the benefit to
the field would be in creating a new interpretation of F. nucleatum sensu lato that
excludes F. animalis and F. watanabei, when there is already an established and widely
understood F. nucleatum sensu lato framework that includes these lineages?
- What is the practical or conceptual upside of redefining an existing and historically
consistent umbrella term in this way? If the intention is to describe or analyze a subset
of species within the F. nucleatum complex, would it not be clearer and less disruptive
to the existing literature to introduce a new, unambiguous term for this more restricted
grouping, rather than altering the meaning of F. nucleatum sensu lato?
- Something like “F. nucleatum core group”?, or similar, where is unlikely to collide
with the established framework. It would be most beneficial if this could be then
included in the figures, where the F.n sensu lato group and this new tighter group are
all clearly highlighted in the main figures for future references. (so Fn sensu lato, Fn.
core group, and Fn sensu stricto would all be in use, but distinguishable)
- This reviewer would strongly advocate for such an alternative choice as currently it
risks creating parallel usages of the same term with different inclusivity. i.e: F.
nucleatum sensu lato = the four canonical subspecies nucleatum, polymorphum,
vincentii, and animalis and their derivative lineages (including F. watanabei)…….but
also F.nucleatum sensu lato = (canonical subspecies nucleatum, polymorphum,
vincentii).
- Further, this redefinition raises another issue. F. animalis has long been considered a
bona fide member of the F. nucleatum sensu lato and already included in this way within
hundreds of studies linking Fusobacterium diversity to disease. Reassigning F. animalis
(and F. watanabei) outside of F. nucleatum sensu lato without a clear taxonomic or
translational rationale risks severing continuity with a decade of literature that used F.
nucleatum sensu lato precisely to unify these lineages under a single, interpretable
construct.
At present, this reviewer cannot discern any clear benefit or added utility to the field in
redefining F. nucleatum sensu lato in this new way. Doing so may increase confusion
among researchers, clinicians, and data curators who have relied on the inclusive sensu
lato framework for consistent comparative and meta-analytical interpretation.
If the authors believe there is genuine conceptual or practical value in excluding F.
animalis and F. watanabei from F. nucleatum sensu lato, could they please elaborate
and articulate that rationale explicitly in the manuscript (what new clarity does this
bring, and to whom?) Otherwise, I apologize, but the proposed redefinition appears to
introduce new complexity without a tangible scientific or translational gain.
Answer: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their appreciation of our work and for this
exceptionally thorough, careful, and thoughtful comment!!! Clearly, our phrasing in the
manuscript caused an unintended and significant misunderstanding, and we deeply
apologise for this.
We would like to clarify that we fully acknowledge and consistently support the
widely-recognised concept of F. nucleatum sensu lato and had absolutely no intention
to redefine it. We have comprehensively revised the entire manuscript to eliminate this
confusion (e.g. lines 171-174 and Table 2). We have clearly stated that F. nucleatum
sensu lato includes the four canonical subspecies nucleatum, polymorphum, vincentii,
and animalis and their derivative lineage F. watanabei. Also, as our own results confirm,
there is no conceptual or practical value in excluding F. animalis and F. watanabei from
F. nucleatum sensu lato. We are truly sorry that our original phrasing and presentation
inadvertently created ambiguity.
We are profoundly grateful to the reviewer for catching this critical issue, which
allows us to improve the clarity of our manuscript. Beyond correcting this specific point,
all the reviewer’s comprehensive perspective and insightful suggestions have also
strengthened the overall impact of our study. Their guidance greatly helped us address
concerns from other reviewers more effectively!
Minor comments:
1. Lines 252–255 “Critically, our evidence supports the argument that the current
subspecies/clade designations under ‘F. nucleatum’ (sensu lato) are taxonomically
invalid.
The phrasing here could be perceived as a little aggressive, implying that prior
taxonomic frameworks are incorrect or invalid, which is inconsistent with taxonomic
freedom and the evolving and interpretive nature of bacterial taxonomy noted early in
the discussion by the authors. Names and classifications reflect the data and consensus
available at the time, but do not become invalid with the emergence of new evidence.
The authors data clearly demonstrates that the historical F. nucleatum sensu lato
subspecies exhibit genomic and phenotypic divergence consistent with species-level
distinctions. However, rather than characterizing existing designations as
“taxonomically invalid,” a more accurate and constructive framing might be that these
designations may no longer adequately capture the observed diversity and that the
authors’ analyses support recognition of these lineages as distinct species under a
revised framework. This would keep the scientific strength of the findings but with a
more balanced tone.
Answer: We agree with the reviewer. Thank you so much for this kind and thoughtful
suggestion! We have realised that the expression was unnecessarily strong and did not
acknowledge their historical context and utility. We have revised the phrasing in the
manuscript to adopt a more accurate and constructive tone as suggested (lines 340-344):
2. Line 62: Notably, the status of Fna C1 remains inconclusive, as it was recently
regrouped with F. vincentii in a metagenomic study
Some additional context may be useful for this particularly unusual lineage that has
quickly changed. The KCOM strains representing the majority of the lineage Fna C1
(21 of 24) were original annotated as Fna/Fa isolates by the Korean Collection for Oral

In this introduction, the authors note that Piccinno G et al determined this lineage to be
clustered with Fnv. It may be useful to readers for Bi et al to elaborate on why this
lineage appears to fluctuate across studies, inherently based on the differences in the
datasets and methods used (16s rRNA vs partial genome vs whole genome vs SGBs of
metagenomes)?
Answer: Thank you very much for this very constructive comment and for providing
such a detailed context regarding Fna C1. This information is particularly useful for

## Abstract

The genus Fusobacterium encompasses significant pathogens implicated in diseases spanning from infections to cancer. However, taxonomic ambiguities persist within the genus, particularly concerning Fusobacterium nucleatum (sensu lato). Through genus-wide average nucleotide identity (ANI) and phylogenetic analyses of 540 Fusobacterium genomes, we identify an ANI gap (93.38%--93.89%) for species delineation, leading to comprehensive taxonomic revisions that resolve these ambiguities. This work establishes a unified taxonomic framework and enabTles standardised species classification for Fusobacterium isolates and microbiomes, highlightinAg the genetic divergence among Fusobacterium species and providing the taxonomic precision essential for advancing Fusobacterium-related research.
